title: Math Practice Isn’t Like Practice in Sports or Music but It Should Be
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer answers defenders of math fluency drills who reach for basketball, carpentry and music analogies by arguing that those disciplines actually develop fluency very differently from a drill sheet. He cites TIMSS data to say fluency is not neglected in US classrooms, so the issue is the quality of practice rather than its quantity. He identifies three gaps: drill sheets give poor feedback, isolate students, and conceal the performance of mathematics that practice is meant to serve. Using Steph Curry's shooting drills, he argues for practice that blends with performance, and points to games, Open Middle tasks and variation theory as examples. The conclusion is that drill sheets also teach a distorted view of what mathematics is. It fits Learning & Curriculum as an argument about practice design.
points: Meyer rejects the premise that fluency needs defending, citing TIMSS data that the US leads the world in students working problems.
The sports and music analogies backfire because those fields supply rich feedback to the practicer, while a drill sheet returns almost none.
Drill sheets are lonely, whereas carpentry, basketball and music practice are often social or observed.
Students rarely have a strong picture of the performance of mathematics, so drill does not feel purposeful the way practice does in sports or music.
Good practice blends fluency with performance, as with Curry's game-movement drills, and tasks like Open Middle and Garbage try to do this for math.
quotes: When you whack a nail into a board or take a jump shot or press a key, the world returns to you a bounty of information about your efforts. Is the nail crooked? How many swings did you need?

If carpentry or basketball or music were like the drill sheet, you’d shoot a shot and the ball would disappear as it left your hand. The nail would evaporate on contact with the hammer. You’d press the piano keys and hear nothing.

It’s possible to work on a carpentry project by yourself or shoot drills alone in a gym. But those are less common than working with someone on a project, participating in group drills, or, at least, observing other people doing their drills, gaining inspiration and knowledge from others.

Define the performance of math however you want and ask yourself, first, how well do your students understand it? Have they watched other people play math? Have they messed around clumsily with math themselves?

Rather, he’s moving between positions as he would in the performance of basketball. He’s trying to do it quickly because the performance of basketball (unlike the performance of math) is timed and requires speed.
